title: El Niño Raises Kerala Dengue Risk, IITM Study Finds; Cases Could Rise 20% by 2040
excerpt: A 14-year IITM analysis links Pacific warming to Kerala's dengue years — and the forecasting model behind it could warn health authorities five months ahead.
body:
• A new study led by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology finds El Niño years are linked to higher dengue incidence in Kerala, analysing 14 years of disease and climate data from 2006 to 2019.
  • Warmer Pacific waters create warmer, drier pre-monsoon conditions in Kerala that favour mosquito breeding before monsoon-season outbreaks.
  • A machine-learning model built from the findings explains 72% of monthly dengue variation and can forecast risk three to five months ahead.
  • The model projects climate-driven dengue cases could rise 16-20% by 2040, and up to 113% by century's end under high emissions — as Kerala battles a severe season with 7,188 cases from June to August.

The Pacific Ocean may be driving Kerala's dengue seasons. A study led by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) in Pune has found a clear link between El Niño years and higher dengue incidence in the state, opening the door to forecasting outbreaks months before they strike.

Published in the journal GeoHealth, the study analysed 14 years of dengue and climate data from Kerala between 2006 and 2019. The finding: Kerala's high-dengue years coincided with El Niño, while mild years fell in La Niña years. Warmer Pacific waters were associated with warmer and relatively drier pre-monsoon conditions in Kerala — exactly the environment in which Aedes mosquitoes breed before cases surge during the monsoon.

A forecast, not just a correlation

The researchers, led by Sophia Yacob and Dr Roxy Mathew Koll with ICMR's National Institute of Translational Virology and AIDS Research and Savitribai Phule Pune University, built a machine-learning model that turns the climate link into a forecasting tool. The model explains 72% of the monthly variation in dengue cases across the state.

Its lead time is what matters for public health. Pacific sea-surface temperatures correlate with Kerala's dengue incidence roughly three months in advance; adding local humidity and temperature data extends the window to nearly five months — enough time to pre-position beds, diagnostics and fogging teams.

"In our model-based analysis, Kerala's high dengue years coincided with El Niño, while mild dengue years fell in La Niña years."

— Dr Roxy Mathew Koll, IITM

A grim present, a worse projection

The study lands mid-crisis. Kerala is enduring a severe dengue season, with 7,188 confirmed cases between June and August — about 60% above the decade-long average for the same period, according to the state directorate of health services. The researchers caution that the study period ended in 2019 and cannot directly attribute this year's surge to the current El Niño, but the historical pattern mirrors present conditions.

The forward projections are sobering. The model suggests climate-driven dengue cases in Kerala could increase by 16-20% by 2040, and by up to 113% by the end of the century under a high-emissions scenario. A separate analysis published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found warming has already increased dengue's toll across Asia and the Americas.

The data problem

There is a catch. Effective early-warning systems depend on health departments sharing data — and Koll has said cooperation is hard to get. "We conducted this study and prepared an early warning system using health data shared by Pune's health department. We approached Kerala and other states where dengue cases are high, but their health departments did not cooperate," he told The Hindu BusinessLine. Dengue is also significantly underreported in India, with actual cases possibly up to 282 times higher than reported figures.

For Kerala's health planners, the science is ready. The question is whether the bureaucracy will let it be used.
